passage:
Monday: Sudha and Uma both grabbed the swing chains in the colony park and yelled until Uma's mother came.
Wednesday: Sudha had an idea. "You push me, then I push you. Ten pushes each." Uma counted ten, then they swapped.
Saturday: Uma ran to the swing first, then stopped. "Ten each?" she asked. Sudha grinned and started pushing.

qa.q: How many pushes did they agree on?
qa.a: Ten pushes each.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling on Wednesday when she had her idea?
qa.a: She felt hopeful and clever, tired of the yelling on Monday.

qa.q: What else could the girls try if a third child wanted a turn?
qa.a: They could count ten pushes for each of the three children, taking turns in a circle.

qa.q: How does the change look to Uma?
qa.a: Uma likes the fair deal so much that she suggests it herself by Saturday.

grounding: Over several days two children move from fighting over a swing to taking turns with a fair count of pushes.

passage: Only one swing was working at the school park, and the bell would ring soon. Uday and Alka reached it together. "Me!" "No, me!" Uday let go. "You push me, then I push you. Fifteen each, fast." Alka counted fast; at fifteen Uday jumped off and pushed her. The bell rang on Alka's fourteenth push. "Almost fair," she laughed.

qa.q: On which push did the bell ring for Alka?
qa.a: On Alka's fourteenth push.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling when she laughed?
qa.a: She was cheerful and content, happy that the swap was nearly fair.

qa.q: What else could Uday and Alka try if the time were even shorter?
qa.a: They could do fewer pushes each, like ten, so both finish before the bell.

qa.q: How does Uday's offer look to Alka?
qa.a: Alka finds it fair and quick, so she agrees and counts fast.

grounding: Two children agree to push each other in turns with a fair count, so both get a turn on the only swing.

passage: I'm Sarika, and Pranav is in my class. At recess the slide line was long. Pranav squeezed past four children and grabbed the ladder. Everyone shouted, "Pranav! No pushing!" He slid down fast. But after that, when he went to the sandpit, the others turned their backs. I don't know if he felt sorry. He played alone the rest of recess, kicking sand.

qa.q: How many children did Pranav squeeze past?
qa.a: Four children.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling as she watched Pranav play alone?
qa.a: Sarika was unsure and a little sorry for him, not knowing if he felt sorry.

qa.q: What else could Pranav try next time?
qa.a: Wait his turn, or ask someone, "Can I go after you?", so his friends don't turn away.

qa.q: What might recess have been like for Pranav after pushing in?
qa.a: He got a quick slide but was then shut out, so he was probably lonely and cross, kicking sand alone.

grounding: An observer describes a child who pushes to the front of the slide line, gets a quick turn, and is shut out by his friends.

passage:
Tuesday: Siami squeezed past everyone to the slide ladder. Hansa shouted, "Cheat!" Siami slid anyway.
Thursday: Siami asked Hansa to play. Hansa said, "No, you push in."
Friday: Siami stood in line behind six children. She waited, arms folded, until her turn. Then she looked at Hansa. "I waited," she said. Hansa shrugged, then smiled.

qa.q: How many children were in front of Siami on Friday?
qa.a: Six children.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling on Tuesday when she shouted "Cheat!"?
qa.a: Hansa was angry that Siami pushed ahead.

qa.q: What went wrong on Tuesday, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Pushing in got Siami one quick turn but cost her Hansa's trust; waiting in line on Friday started to fix it.

qa.q: How might Siami feel on Thursday when Hansa says no?
qa.a: Siami would likely feel hurt and surprised that one quick turn cost her a friend.

grounding: Over several days a child learns that pushing to the front of the line costs her a friendship, and begins waiting her turn.

passage:
Note for Kunal's parents
At recess today the swing line was long. Kunal stood in it for a moment, then walked to the corner by the water tank and said loudly, "I don't want to play anyway." He sat with his back to the swings. I noticed he watched the swings over his shoulder. I asked if he'd like to join the line with me, and we waited together.

qa.q: Where did Kunal walk to?
qa.a: To the corner by the water tank.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he said "I don't want to play anyway"?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and impatient, pretending not to care to hide it.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do, and why might it help?
qa.a: They offered to wait in line with him, which made the waiting feel easier and got him a turn.

qa.q: How might Kunal's parents feel reading this?
qa.a: They might feel sympathetic and glad someone noticed his feelings behind the words.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child who walks off from a long line saying he doesn't want to play, protecting his feelings and missing his turn.

passage: At the temple fair in Sirsi, the line for the toy train went round the banyan tree. Akash looked at it, kicked a stone and said to his sister Nikita, "I don't even want to go. It's a baby ride." He sat down on the steps. Nikita stayed in line. When she rode past, waving, Akash watched every round, chin on his hands.

qa.q: Where did Akash sit down?
qa.a: On the steps.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling as he watched every round?
qa.a: He was disappointed and wistful, wishing he'd stayed in line.

qa.q: What would you advise Akash next time?
qa.a: Stay in line with Nikita and talk while waiting, because giving up means missing the ride.

qa.q: How might Nikita see Akash on the steps?
qa.a: Nikita might feel a bit sorry for him and guess he really wanted the ride.

grounding: A child walks away from a long line saying he doesn't want to go, which protects his feelings but costs him a turn.

passage:
"My turn! My turn!" Jagdish yelled at the swing, stamping his feet.
Zainab kept swinging. "No!"
"MY TURN!"
"Go away!"
Jagdish kicked the dust and went home.
Next day, he waited by the swing first.
"Zainab, can I go after you?"
Zainab looked at him. "Okay. Five more."
She swung five, then hopped off. "Your go."
Jagdish climbed on and grinned. "Asking works."

qa.q: How many more swings did Zainab take?
qa.a: Five more.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he said "Asking works"?
qa.a: He was pleased and surprised that asking politely got him a turn.

qa.q: What else could Jagdish add to his polite asking?
qa.a: He could offer to push Zainab first, which makes her even more likely to agree.

qa.q: How does the change look to Zainab?
qa.a: Zainab finds the polite question much easier to say yes to than the yelling.

grounding: A child finds that shouting "my turn" gets nowhere, then asks politely the next day and keeps that as his new plan.

passage:
Note for Karthik's parents
On Monday Karthik stood by the swing shouting, "My turn!" at Zubin, who stayed on. Karthik cried. On Tuesday he walked up and said, "Zubin, can I go after you?" Zubin nodded and got off soon after. Karthik looked surprised. Today he asked the same way again. I told him I noticed his polite asking.

qa.q: What did Karthik say on Tuesday?
qa.a: "Zubin, can I go after you?"

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when Zubin got off?
qa.a: He was surprised and pleased that asking worked.

qa.q: What else could the note-writer do to help Karthik keep this plan?
qa.a: They could keep praising his polite asking, so he knows it's a plan that works.

qa.q: How does Karthik's new question look to Zubin?
qa.a: Zubin finds it easy to agree when asked nicely.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child who moves from shouting to politely asking for a turn on the swing and keeps the new plan.

passage: On the colony lawn in Chandigarh, Baljeet had the yellow truck and Parul had the doll with the pink dress. Baljeet kept looking at the doll, his chin on his knees. Parul kept looking at the truck, twisting her plait. "Swap?" Baljeet said, holding out the truck. Parul thought, then handed over the doll. "Only till lunch." Baljeet nodded. They played side by side, each with the other's toy.

qa.q: What colour was the doll's dress?
qa.a: Pink.

qa.q: What was Baljeet thinking when he held out the truck?
qa.a: He felt hopeful that Parul wanted the truck as much as he wanted the doll.

qa.q: What else could Baljeet try if Parul said no?
qa.a: He could offer a turn with the truck while asking for a short turn with the doll.

qa.q: How does the swap look to Parul?
qa.a: Parul finds it fair and fun, since she gets the truck she wanted.

grounding: A child swaps his toy truck for a turn with his friend's doll, and both get something they want.

passage:
"Jeevan, can I play with your doll?" Arnab asked.
"No."
"Please?"
"No, she's mine."
Arnab looked at his truck. "If you give me the doll, you can have the truck."
Jeevan stopped. "The whole truck?"
"Till snack time."
"Okay!"
They swapped. Jeevan zoomed the truck, and Arnab combed the doll's hair.

qa.q: Until when did Arnab offer the truck?
qa.a: Till snack time.

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling when he said "Okay!"?
qa.a: He was happy and excited to get the truck.

qa.q: What else could Arnab offer next time?
qa.a: Playing together with both toys, so neither has to give one up.

qa.q: How does the swap look to Arnab?
qa.a: Arnab is pleased because his offer worked and he got the doll.

grounding: A child swaps his truck for a turn with a friend's doll, and both get something they want.

passage: In the Siliguri flat, Pema clutched her red truck. Binita had a tin of little cars. Pema frowned, thinking. If I give her the truck, she'll give me the cars. She held out the truck. "You can have it. Can I have your cars?" Binita said, "Okay," and pushed the tin across. Pema lined up the cars, smiling.

qa.q: What colour was Pema's truck?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: What was Pema thinking as she frowned?
qa.a: She was working it out, hopeful that giving the truck would get her the cars.

qa.q: What else could Pema do if Binita said no?
qa.a: She could still share the truck, or ask to play with both toys together.

qa.q: How does Pema's offer look to Binita?
qa.a: Binita finds it fair and easy to agree to.

grounding: A child reasons that sharing her truck will lead her friend to share cars, which makes handing it over easier.

passage:
"Naveen, give me the truck!" Lokesh said.
"No."
"You never share."
Naveen looked at Lokesh's bag of cars. He thought out loud, "If I share the truck, then you share your cars?"
"Yes."
"All of them?"
"Five."
"Okay." Naveen handed over the truck, and Lokesh poured out five cars.

qa.q: How many cars did Lokesh pour out?
qa.a: Five cars.

qa.q: What was Naveen thinking when he thought out loud?
qa.a: He felt hopeful that sharing the truck would get him some cars too.

qa.q: What else could Naveen try if Lokesh wouldn't trade?
qa.a: He could suggest playing together so both toys are shared.

qa.q: How does Naveen's rule look to Lokesh?
qa.a: Lokesh finds it fair and agrees, since he gets the truck.

grounding: A child reasons that if he shares his truck, his friend will share cars, which makes sharing less costly.

passage: The kindergarten was noisy with rain outside and every child indoors. Uma and Kishore both pulled the toy xylophone. "Mine!" "Mine!" Uma finally went to the teacher. "Ma'am, he won't let go." The teacher brought a small sand timer. "When the sand runs out, it's the other person's turn." Uma played first. When the last grain dropped, she handed it to Kishore without a fuss.

qa.q: What did the teacher bring?
qa.a: A small sand timer.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she handed over the xylophone?
qa.a: She seemed calm and fair, ready to follow the timer.

qa.q: What else could Uma try before going to the teacher?
qa.a: She could suggest taking turns herself, like counting to twenty each.

qa.q: How does the timer look to Kishore?
qa.a: Kishore gets a clear, fair turn, which probably feels better than pulling.

grounding: Two children tug a toy until one asks the teacher, who suggests a sand timer, and the child follows it.

passage: At the Mumbai playschool, Ishita and Gargi both yanked the play dough cutters. "Ma'am!" Ishita called. The teacher came over, holding a tiny sand timer. "Each of you has one timer. When the sand runs out, give the cutters over." Ishita watched the sand trickle. When the last bit fell, she held out the cutters to Gargi. "Your turn."

qa.q: What was the teacher holding?
qa.a: A tiny sand timer.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as she watched the sand?
qa.a: She was probably eager and patient, knowing her turn had a clear end.

qa.q: What else could Ishita try if there were no timer?
qa.a: She could count to a number, like fifty, and swap.

qa.q: How does the timer look to Gargi?
qa.a: Gargi finds it fair and knows her turn is coming.

grounding: Two children pull on a toy until a teacher suggests a sand timer, and the child follows the timer's rule.

passage:
Playschool note for Ramesh's parents
Today Payal asked to hold Ramesh's toy robot. He said, "No! If you touch it, it will stop working." He hid it in his bag. When I asked why, he whispered, "It gets used up." I held the robot, then gave it back working, and he checked it carefully. He still did not share today.

qa.q: Where did Ramesh hide the robot?
qa.a: In his bag.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when he hid the robot?
qa.a: He was afraid and worried the robot would stop working if Payal touched it.

qa.q: What else could help Ramesh feel safer sharing?
qa.a: Letting Payal hold it for a short time with him watching, so he can see it still works.

qa.q: How does the hiding look to Payal?
qa.a: Payal feels left out and confused, since she only wanted to hold it.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child who hides his toy because he fears it will be used up if a friend touches it.

passage: In the kasba lane, Ankita had a new spinning top from the fair. Omkar asked, "Can I spin it?" Ankita pulled it close. "No! If you spin it, it won't spin for me anymore." She hid it under her frock and ran home. Omkar stood in the lane. Later, Ankita spun it alone in the courtyard. It spun just the same.

qa.q: Where did Ankita hide the top?
qa.a: Under her frock.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she hid the top?
qa.a: She was afraid and worried that Omkar would use up the spin.

qa.q: What would you change first to help Ankita?
qa.a: Let Omkar try it once with her watching, so she sees the top still spins.

qa.q: How does the hiding look to Omkar?
qa.a: Omkar is disappointed and left standing, not understanding why she ran.

grounding: A child hides her new top, fearing it will stop working if a friend touches it.

passage: In the small school in Sangli, Kalyani saw Anjali hand her green crayon to the new girl. The new girl smiled and let Anjali use her paints. Kalyani watched. Later, she passed her own blue crayon to Anjali. "Here." Anjali smiled and pushed the paint box toward her. Kalyani dipped a brush, grinning.

qa.q: What colour was Kalyani's crayon?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she dipped the brush?
qa.a: She was happy and pleased that copying Anjali worked.

qa.q: What else could Kalyani do to keep sharing?
qa.a: She could offer crayons first to others too, since giving tends to bring giving back.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Kalyani gives her the crayon?
qa.a: Anjali probably feels friendly and glad to share her paints in return.

grounding: A child sees a classmate share a crayon and get a turn with paints, then does the same and it works.

passage: At the Oslo school, Amara saw Lars give a crayon to the girl beside him. She smiled and let him use her watercolours. Amara looked down at her own crayons. When the girl with the paints glanced her way, Amara held out a purple crayon. The girl smiled and slid the paint box over. Amara painted a purple cat.

qa.q: What did Amara paint?
qa.a: A purple cat.

qa.q: What was Amara feeling when she held out the crayon?
qa.a: She was hopeful and a little shy, trying what worked for Lars.

qa.q: What else could Amara try if the girl said no?
qa.a: She could still share and ask for a paint turn later.

qa.q: How does the swap look to the girl with the paints?
qa.a: The girl finds it friendly and fair, so she smiles and shares.

grounding: A child watches a classmate share a crayon and get a turn with paints, then copies it and succeeds.

passage: Payal's cousin Gopika was leaving in an hour, and she wanted to play with Payal's toy telephone. Payal clutched it. Then she had an idea. "This is my shop. You can borrow it, but you have to bring it back when the shop closes." Gopika nodded. "The shop closes when Mummy calls." Gopika played; when Mummy called, she returned it.

qa.q: When did the shop close?
qa.a: When Mummy called.

qa.q: What was Payal thinking when she said "This is my shop"?
qa.a: She felt safer and more in control, knowing the phone would come back.

qa.q: What else could Payal try if Gopika forgot?
qa.a: She could remind Gopika gently about closing time.

qa.q: How does the shop game look to Gopika?
qa.a: Gopika enjoys it and gets to play with the phone.

grounding: A child turns sharing into a shop game where her cousin borrows the toy and returns it at closing time.

passage: On the balcony of their Kolkata flat, Jahnavi set up a shop with her doll. Deepak asked, "Can I have the doll?" Jahnavi said, "You're the customer. You can borrow it till the shop closes." "When does it close?" "When the shadow reaches the pot." Deepak played. When the shadow touched the pot, he brought it back. "Shop's closed!"

qa.q: When did Jahnavi's shop close?
qa.a: When the shadow reaches the pot.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi thinking when she made Deepak a customer?
qa.a: She felt safe and happy knowing the doll would come back.

qa.q: What else could Jahnavi try with other toys?
qa.a: She could use the same game to share her other toys.

qa.q: How does the shop game look to Deepak?
qa.a: Deepak finds it fun and fair, so he returns the doll on time.

grounding: A child turns sharing into a shop game where her friend borrows the doll until closing time.
